units.translation: 1a. 〈There:〉 on the shore, where they had moored. Lm
b. αὖλις is the stay and the sojourn. Lm (P)
c. Amycus was king of the Bebryces, a Bithynian people. Lm

2a. King of the Bebryces: Amycus was king of the Bebryces, who at that time occupied the rest of Bithynia and its coastal regions. Some of them also settled around Lydia in the places near Ephesus and Magnesia. Charon (fr. 7 M. I 33) says that the territory of the Lampsacenes was formerly called Bebrycia after the Bebryces who settled it. Their race has been wiped out by the wars that occurred, just as other peoples have.
b. 〈ἀγήνορος:〉 arrogant. Lg
c. ἀγήνορα means the haughty one. P

3-4a. Bithynian Melie: it is unclear whether it is a proper name. He calls her Melia either because some of the nymphs are called Meliae after Melia the daughter of Oceanus, as Callimachus says (fr. 404 Schn.), or because they spend their time among ash trees like the Hamadryads; and Bithynian because she happens to be Bithynian by birth. 〈...〉 He called him Genethlius because he rules over moisture and is the cause of all nourishment and generation, inasmuch as water is generative of all things.

Melia the daughter of Oceanus, as Callimachus says (fr. 404 Schn.), or because they spend their time among ash trees like the Hamadryads; and Bithynian because she happens to be Bithynian by birth. 〈...〉 He called him Genethlius because he rules over moisture and is the cause of all nourishment and generation, inasmuch as water is generative of all things.
b. Bithynian: a proper name. Lg (P)
c. Melie: an epithet. Lg (P)
d. ὑπεροπληέστατον: most arrogant. Lg (P)
5. Who also established an evil law against strangers. Lg
10 6. ἀποστείχειν: to depart. Lg P
8-10a. And then: the sense: and then, coming to the ship, he did not care to ask about the needs of their voyage, that is, what they needed and who they were, but spoke such words to them. L

b. χρειώ μιν ἐρέσϑαι: the μιν is singular instead of plural, meaning them, the heroes. But it can also be singular, so that we take it as referring to Amycus: for he—Amycus—had to ask the heroes. Theocritus (XXII 53 sq.) tells the story differently.
c. ὄτισεν stands for 'he did not care'; for what one does not honor, one does not care about. P
20 d. παρασχεδόν stands for 'near'. P
12-14. ϑέσμιον: lawful. The meaning: it is a law that no stranger who lands in Bebrycia may depart before boxing with me. L
15-16a. τῷ καί μοι: therefore, having chosen the best of you, set him to contend with me in boxing. L
b. ἀποκριδόν stands for 'by selection'. P
c. δηρινϑῆναι stands for 'to fight', from δηρίνομαι; and this from δηρίομαι. P

17-18. εἰ δ’ ἂν ἀπηλεγέοντες: being heedless, considering it as nothing. 〈...〉 Herodian says ἀνηλεγέως with ν in the sixth book of the Katholike (I 79, 23 L.). The sense: if you disregard my laws and consider them as nothing, you will suffer, I think, no ordinary compulsion.
19. 〈μέγα φρονέων:〉 as if beyond human. Lg
